meta.title: Who really said "Uncontrolled variation is the enemy of quality"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely credited to W. Edwards Deming, but no primary source exists. The trail ends at a statistics textbook, and the Deming Institute does not list it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Uncontrolled variation is the enemy of quality'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to W. Edwards Deming everywhere, sourced nowhere. The citation trail ends in a textbook epigraph, not in anything Deming published.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Deming, and squarely inside the subject he spent his life on — but no primary source pins the wording to him. The only citation anyone offers is a secondary one: a Wiley statistics textbook by Kang and Kvam, page 19, which credits Deming without naming a work. The Deming Institute’s own page-cited quote database does not list the line at all.

source.heading: The source that isn’t there

docMeta.dd: Basic Statistical Tools for Improving Quality, p. 19

source.excerpt: Uncontrolled variation is the enemy of quality.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ has never taken this one up. Site searches for “uncontrolled variation” and for “enemy of quality” both return no matches, so there is no specialist finding to defer to here.

Wikiquote’s Deming page ↗ does carry the line — but in its loose opening list, not in any of the sourced sections for Out of the Crisis, Some Theory of Sampling or The New Economics. Its note reads: “Attributed to Edward Deming (1980) in: Chang W. Kang, Paul H. Kvam (2012) Basic Statistical Tools for Improving Quality. p. 19.”

The Deming Institute cites its own quote database ↗ to the page — Out of the Crisis, Some Theory of Sampling, named seminars, dated interviews. Across all eleven pages of that database the words “enemy” and “uncontrolled” do not appear once.

Even the careful downstream users hedge. Health Catalyst’s piece on clinical variation says Deming “is credited as stating” ↗ the line, and points to the same textbook rather than to anything Deming wrote.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller context to show. The sentence has never been traced to a lecture, a seminar transcript, an article or a book of Deming’s — it circulates only as a free-standing epigraph.
source.rightsNote: Because no work has been identified as the source, no copyright status can honestly be claimed for this wording. Worth noting either way: every book Deming published — from Statistical Adjustment of Data (1943) through Out of the Crisis and The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education (1993), as listed on Wikipedia ↗ — appeared well after 1930. If the line were ever traced to one of them, it would be in copyright, not public domain.

author.name: W. Edwards Deming
author.kicker: About the man it is pinned on
author.heading: Who was W. Edwards Deming?
author.bio: W. Edwards Deming was an American statistician who worked on sampling theory and statistical quality control before delivering his celebrated 1950 lectures on statistical product quality administration in Japan. He remained little known at home until NBC’s 1980 documentary If Japan Can... Why Can’t We? made him a management figure in the United States, after which he wrote Out of the Crisis and The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education and ran his four-day seminars until his death. His central teaching was the System of Profound Knowledge, in which understanding variation is one of four parts that cannot be separated from the others.

misattribution.heading: Credited everywhere, sourced nowhere
misattribution.intro: Nobody disputes that Deming spent his career on variation. What is missing is this sentence, in his voice, on a dated page. Every trail runs into the same short loop.

items.why: Wikiquote’s note ↗ renders his name as “Edward Deming,” gives a bare year, and then points not to Deming at all but to a Wiley statistics textbook by Chang W. Kang and Paul H. Kvam, page 19. No lecture, seminar or publication of that year is identified.

A widely read process-management explainer quotes the line and hyperlinks it to the Deming Institute’s own “Knowledge of Variation” ↗ article as if that were the receipt. That article never uses the words “enemy” or “uncontrolled.”
QuotePark reproduces the same Wikiquote line verbatim and then, in effect, admits the gap by asking readers to “help us to complete the source” ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest ceiling is the one Health Catalyst reaches for: Deming “is credited as stating” ↗ it. Credited — not documented.

context.heading: He did teach this. Just not in these words.
lead: Variation really was Deming’s subject. Building on Walter Shewhart’s control charts, he taught managers to separate ordinary, built-in variation from genuine special causes, and warned that reacting to the ordinary kind — tampering — only makes a system perform worse. He carried that teaching to Japan in his 1950 lectures on statistical product quality administration, and was still teaching it in four-day seminars four decades later.

So the slogan lands on the right target and still misses the shot. “Uncontrolled variation is the enemy of quality” compresses a distinction into a villain. Deming’s point was rarely that variation is an enemy; it was that variation is information, and that the real failure is not reading it.
detailsBody: What Deming did put on the record, cited to the book: in The New Economics for Industry, Government, Education he asks, “What is the variation trying to tell us about a process, about the people in the process?” — recorded by Wikiquote ↗ under that book’s own heading, unlike the sentence on this page.

Understanding variation was never meant to stand alone. It is one of the four inseparable parts of Deming’s System of Profound Knowledge, alongside appreciation for a system, theory of knowledge and psychology, as the Deming Institute sets it out ↗. A one-line slogan about controlling variation is precisely the sort of tool-without-theory shortcut he spent his last years arguing against.
context.pull: The line sounds exactly like Deming. The footnote never arrives.
